in-fŏdĭo , fōdi, fossum, 3, v. a.,
I.to dig in or up, make by digging; to bury in the earth, inter: “locus alte duos pedes infodiendus est,” Col. 3, 13, 5 : “sarmenta,” Cato, R. R. 37, 3 : “squalentes conchas,” Verg. G. 2, 348 corpora terrae, id. A. 11, 205: “taleas in terram,” Caes. B. G. 7, 73 : “procul ab eo loco infoderunt, in quo erat mortuus,” Nep. Paus. 5 : gemmas corpori (sc. auribus), to insert in,
Plin. 12, prooem. § “2: vulnera infossa penitus cerebro,” inflicted deeply, Stat. Th. 8, 534 : “saxum perfractae cassidis aera Ossibus infodiens,” Sil. 10, 238 : “infossus puer,” buried, Hor. Epod. 5, 32 .
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
